claim: On 200 AITA posts, asking Jev the verdict directly scored 53.0% while decomposing into eight yes/no fact questions scored 41.5% (hand rule) or 51.5% (learned rule).
quote: On 200 older posts, asking directly got 53.0% right. Asking eight yes/no questions about the facts, then turning the answers into a verdict, got 41.5% with a hand-written rule and 51.5% with a rule learned from data.
why: Direct counter-evidence to 'always decompose'; measured on labelled data

claim: In the 770-post AITA run, Jev's two-yes/no-question setup had weighted Brier 0.515 vs 0.369 for the single direct Choice question, i.e. decomposition badly hurt calibration.
why: Shows combining two Noul probabilities into a 4-way verdict degrades Brier vs one Choice (direct row 0.369)

claim: Lindfors found rewriting Jev Noul questions into longer 'careful' wording with qualifiers raised ECE from 0.040 to 0.116, moved 24->41 judgments into the 0.3-0.7 bin, and cut agreement 0.89->0.86.
quote: Then I wrote the label guide and rewrote the questions to match it, with the qualifiers about passing mentions and quotations. ... The longer instruction pushed the probabilities toward the middle.
why: Key evidence that long qualified instructions hurt calibration; small n (192 judgments, 24 docs, frontier-model labels)

claim: Kumar found Jev 96-98% accurate on simple page-type yes/no gates but only 68.6% on 'does this page carry a value for one of 135 report rows', where it fires on mentions and swung 0.5 between runs.
quote: "Does this page carry a value for one of 135 report rows" means telling apart a mention of something from an actual value for it, and Jev fires on the mention. ... its probability swung by 0.5 between runs on the same page.
why: Mention-vs-value failure mode directly relevant to scoring whether evidence cards contain a claim vs merely mention it; also notes long input / business-logic questions lower accuracy

claim: JevBench records Jev phishing recall moving from 85.7% (text-only prompt) to 98.4% (enriched evidence criteria) on the same 5,733-email set, and 43.2% on a different set with a text-only protocol.
quote: 85.7% Phishing recall, text-only prompt 98.4% Same set, same model, enriched evidence 43.2% A different set, text-only protocol ... The gap between the first two is nothing but the prompt
why: Quantifies prompt/criteria sensitivity; caveat: enriched criteria were informed by labelled errors (not zero-shot)

claim: An arXiv study found that on Jev, swapping which definition is bound to yes/no option names flips 32.5% of decisions (30.4 pp above 0/1 names) and drops balanced accuracy 71.3%->51.6%; neutral/random names flip ~2%.
quote: On Jev, evaluated on the same 1,200 questions as Laya, yes/ no flips 32.5% of the decisions, 30.4 pp more than 0/ 1 (95% CI [27.6, 33.3]); balanced accuracy falls from 71.3% to 51.6%, and AUC from 81.5% to 58.1%.
why: Option names override option definitions: Choice keys must agree with their criteria text; preprint, not peer reviewed

claim: Keyi Li's coherence test found Jev's P('label is X') and P('label is not X') miss summing to 1 by 0.064 on average, its three single-label Nouls sum to 1.14, and Noul vs Choice probabilities for the same label differ by 0.09.
quote: Jev gives single-label statements an average probability of 0.380 where coherence requires 1/3, which also makes its three single-label probabilities sum to 1.14. Its yes/no and choice probabilities for the same label differ by 0.09
why: Negation phrasing and question form change probabilities; violations concentrate where Jev is uncertain; preprint

claim: Sys1Cal-v1 found Jev's Choice probabilities worse calibrated than Noul or Score on the same items (mean OVL 0.764 vs 0.918 Noul, 0.886 Score), with Choice less invariant to equivalent formulations.
quote: Our evaluation shows that Jev's primitives do not expose probability in the same way. Noul and Score are substantially better aligned with the ground-truth probabilities than Choice. The benchmark also reveals representation sensitivity
why: Bears on question-type choice when the probability itself is consumed (e.g., card relevance scores); synthetic data, preprint

claim: In backnotprop's poker eval, five option phrasings matched the solver on the same 63% of spots, but value-laden verbs pushed Jev toward bigger bets; decomposed designs (six judgments+code, regret-per-action, six facts) scored 57-59% vs 63% for one question.
quote: Option labels carry no framing. Five phrasings over 30 spots, including "which action makes hero the most money in the long run" and no labels at all, matched the solver on the same 63% of spots. Value-laden verbs pushed Jev toward bigger bets
why: Evidence on loaded wording in option labels and mixed results for decomposition (helped facing-bet spots 71% vs 62%); single board, solver agreement

claim: A dev.to benchmark found tightening Jev criteria lifted a shell-risk gate from 66.2% to 78.5% agreement, decomposition+code cut false positives 14.5%->1.8%, and a merged 'pressure vs legitimate escalation' question gave 0.47 vs 0.04/0.96 when split.
quote: Criteria are the decision boundary. Merge "pressure" and "legitimate escalation" into one question and you get a mushy 0.47; split them and you get 0.04 / 0.96.
why: Supports one-criterion-per-question and explicit criteria; also: per-candidate Nouls without competition cluster near 0.5 (top-10 mean 0.56)

claim: OpenRouter found Jev matched an LLM judge on a closed-rubric faithfulness set (84/88, Brier 0.043) but trailed badly on open-rubric SummEval consistency (Spearman 0.47 vs 0.72); padding wrong answers raised Jev's mean P(acceptable) 0.08->0.12.
quote: Coherence is a tie. Consistency, the criterion you care about when you are hunting hallucinations, is a clear win for the LLM judge. ... Jev has to do it in one pass over roughly 1,000 tokens of state.
why: Closed rubrics with evidence in state work; claim-by-claim consistency over long text does not; verbosity bias small

claim: In OpenRouter's 3,080-item Banking77 run, both Jev and Opus 5 scored 0/40 on get_physical_card because option criteria were written from label names only without example messages.
quote: both models stumbled on one class, because the criteria were written from label names only, without seeing example messages. ... Each model scored 0 out of 40 on that class, routing most messages to `change_pin` instead.
why: Shows option descriptions need concrete boundary content, not names; also confidence >=0.99 gave 96.3% accuracy

claim: Jevals measured 10.3% of Jev's Banking77 picks changing when Choice options were reordered, versus 2.7% on an identical rerun, so option order matters beyond nondeterminism.
quote: Stability 2.7% of answers change on an identical rerun · 10.3% change when options are reordered
why: Option ordering sensitivity number; 77-option task, operator anonymous

claim: Every's Mike Taylor ran 21 AI-tell yes/no questions (e.g. 'Does the text repeat an idea without adding evidence?') across 37 docs; Shipper's four defect checks caught 6 of 7 planted defects vs Fable's 7.
quote: The checks asked whether an action was unexplained, a reasoning link was missing, a mechanism had replaced the intended outcome, or a claim distorted its source.
why: Example wordings of writing-quality Nouls; no accuracy measurement for the 21-question sweep, tiny n for the 4 checks

claim: A third-party wiki cites TypeSafe examples where Nouls on 'refund' and 'not_refund' summed to 1.19 and a Noul gave 0.22 vs a yes/no Choice 0.01 on the same text, advising not to derive 'not X' by asking X.
quote: So do not implement "not X" by asking X and subtracting, and do not ask both and expect them to agree. Word the one question you actually want.
why: Third-party wiki (not TypeSafe); relays TypeSafe jaggedness-page examples on negation and Noul/Choice non-equivalence

claim: OpenRouter's cookbook found a 'celebrity' tag Noul never exceeded 0.41 precision at any threshold because its instruction overlapped with sibling 'music' and 'film_tv' tags.
quote: In the captured run, `celebrity` never passed 0.41 precision because its instruction, `Is the post about a celebrity or pop culture?`, overlaps with `music` and `film_tv`. Tighten the instruction or the criteria
why: Overlapping criteria across questions cap precision; fix the wording, not the threshold
